title: Stable subspaces and the center
statement:
Use the coefficient and matrix-group conventions of [sk-d-geometry]: $L$ is an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, $V,M$ are finite-dimensional $L$-vector spaces, and $G\subseteq\operatorname{GL}(V)$ is a finite-type closed subgroup scheme. Write $D=L[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)$. In the tangent-space convention of [def-wf-lie-algebra-derivation],
$$X\in\operatorname{Lie}(G)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 1+\epsilon X\in G(D).$$
The bracket is $[X,Y]=XY-YX$, and this space is closed under the bracket. For a rational representation $r:G\to\operatorname{GL}(M)$, its differential is characterized by
$$r(1+\epsilon X)=1+\epsilon\,dr(X),$$
and $dr$ is a Lie algebra homomorphism.

If $G$ is connected, a subspace $U\subseteq M$ is $G$-stable (every $g\in G(L)$ preserves $U$) if and only if $dr(X)U\subseteq U$ for every $X\in\operatorname{Lie}(G)$. Moreover,
$$\operatorname{Lie}(Z(G)^\circ)=Z(\operatorname{Lie}(G)).$$
Here $Z(G)$ and $Z(G)^\circ$ are the reduced center and its identity component of [sk-d-geometry], and the Lie center is $\{X:[X,Y]=0\text{ for all }Y\}$ as in [sk-d-lie]. The equality is inside $\operatorname{Lie}(G)$ via the differential of $Z(G)^\circ\hookrightarrow G$. In particular these assertions apply to every connected closed subgroup $G\subseteq\operatorname{GL}_{n,L}$ and every rational representation $r:G\to\operatorname{GL}_{m,L}$, with no faithfulness hypothesis on $r$.

proof.text: Apply [lem-wf-lie-algebra-derivation-bracket] to $G,V,M,r$. It states that the dual-number tangent space is a linear subspace closed under $XY-YX$, and that $dr$ is linear and preserves that bracket. These are exactly the preliminary assertions; neither connectedness nor faithfulness is needed here.

proof.text:
Choose a basis of $M$ whose first $a=\dim U$ vectors span $U$. In $G$, impose that the lower-left $(\dim M-a)\times a$ block of $r(g)$ vanish, and call the resulting closed subscheme $S$. It is a subgroup scheme: block upper triangular invertible matrices have block upper triangular inverses and products. Indeed their two diagonal determinants have invertible product, hence are units over every commutative $L$-algebra. Thus $S$ is a finite-type group scheme. By [lem-sfb-cartier-characteristic-zero-smooth], $S$ and $G$ are smooth and reduced (Stacks Tag 047N, lemma-group-scheme-characteristic-zero-smooth). A tangent vector of $S$ is precisely a tangent vector $1+\epsilon X$ of $G$ for which the lower-left block of $1+\epsilon dr(X)$ vanishes. Comparing coefficients in the free $L$-basis $1,\epsilon$ gives
$$\operatorname{Lie}(S)=\{X\in\operatorname{Lie}(G):dr(X)U\subseteq U\}.$$
This reads the actual defining equations, so no radicalization is used. It also covers $a=0$ and $a=\dim M$, when the block has no entries.

source.place: statement and proof; field convention in sk-i-cartier/_section.md

proof.text: If $U$ is Lie-stable, the preceding formula gives $\operatorname{Lie}(S)=\operatorname{Lie}(G)$. As $G$ is connected and $S$ is a closed subgroup scheme, [sk-p-geometry] gives $S=G$, hence $U$ is $G$-stable. Conversely suppose every $g\in G(L)$ preserves $U$. Each lower-left matrix coefficient of $r$ then vanishes at every $L$-point of the reduced finite-type affine scheme $G$. By the vanishing principle [lem-wf-affine-nullstellensatz-vanishing] these functions are zero in $L[G]$. Thus $S=G$ as schemes, and the same tangent formula gives Lie-stability. This proves the equivalence for arbitrary rational $r$.

source.place: statement and proof; field convention in sk-i-cartier/_section.md

proof.text:
Put $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(G)$. By [lem-sfb-affine-group-centre-base-change], the scheme center $C=C_G(G)$ is a closed subgroup scheme. Cartier's theorem [lem-sfb-cartier-characteristic-zero-smooth] makes $C$ reduced. It agrees with the reduced center $Z(G)$ used in the statement: for $g\in G(L)$ commuting with every $h\in G(L)$, each entry of $gh-hg$, as a regular function of $h$, is zero on all $L$-points, hence identically zero by [lem-wf-affine-nullstellensatz-vanishing]. The commutation identity therefore holds after every scalar extension. This proves $C(L)=Z(G)(L)$; the ideals of two reduced closed subschemes with these points agree by the same vanishing principle on each subscheme. Apply [lem-sfb-lie-normalizer-centralizer-invariants] with $K=G$ and with its auxiliary smooth subgroup $H$ taken to be the trivial group and $N=G$, which normalizes that subgroup. Its centralizer clause gives
$$\operatorname{Lie}(Z(G))=\mathfrak g^G,$$
where the right side consists of vectors fixed by the adjoint action over every commutative $L$-algebra. The auxiliary trivial group is smooth by Cartier, and both $G$ and $C$ are affine of finite type, as that node requires.

source.place: statement and proof; field convention in sk-i-cartier/_section.md

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-lie-normalizer-centralizer-invariants], conjugation induces a rational linear action $\operatorname{Ad}$ of $G$ on $\mathfrak g$, i.e. a homomorphism of group schemes $G\to\operatorname{GL}(\mathfrak g)$, given on $R$-points by $h\mapsto(X\otimes1\mapsto hXh^{-1})$; on $L$-points it is $\operatorname{Ad}(g)X=gXg^{-1}$, and its differential is $d\operatorname{Ad}(Y)X=[Y,X]$ by [def-wf-lie-algebra-derivation]. A vector fixed by the whole group functor is fixed by $1+\epsilon Y$; the identity $(1+\epsilon Y)X(1-\epsilon Y)=X+\epsilon[Y,X]$ gives $[Y,X]=0$, hence it is central. Conversely, for central $X$, use the rational representation $\operatorname{Ad}\oplus1$ on $\mathfrak g\oplus L$. Its differential sends $(X,1)$ to $([Y,X],0)=(0,0)$ for every $Y$. The equivalence just proved makes the line $L(X,1)$ stable under $G(L)$. Since the last coordinate of the image is $1$, the proportionality scalar is $1$, so $\operatorname{Ad}(g)X=X$ for all $g\in G(L)$. Each coordinate of $\operatorname{Ad}(g)X-X$ is a regular function on reduced affine $G$; [lem-wf-affine-nullstellensatz-vanishing] makes it zero in $L[G]$, hence zero after evaluation in every $L$-algebra. Thus $X\in\mathfrak g^G$, proving $\mathfrak g^G=Z(\mathfrak g)$.

source.place: statement and proof; field convention in sk-i-cartier/_section.md

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-locally-algebraic-group-identity-component] to $C=Z(G)$. Its identity component is open and closed, and has the open subgroup-scheme structure. Since $C$ is reduced by step 4, this open subscheme is already reduced, so it is the reduced identity component in the statement. An open neighborhood of the identity has the same local ring there as $C$, hence the same maximal ideal modulo its square. The identity-point cotangent duality [lem-ag-lie-identity-cotangent-dual] identifies the Lie space with the dual of this quotient, using the canonical identity residue-field identification; the tangent-map convention of [def-wf-lie-algebra-derivation] makes the inclusion act by the identity on this unchanged local-ring description. Therefore $\operatorname{Lie}(Z(G)^\circ)=\operatorname{Lie}(Z(G))$. Combining steps 4 and 5 proves the center equality, with both tangent inclusions read inside $\operatorname{Lie}(G)$.

blueprint_update.statement:
For a matrix group $G\subseteq\GL(V)$, define $\Lie(G)$ by its
dual-number points at $1$:

$$
X\in\Lie(G)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
1+\epsilon X\in G(L[\epsilon]/\epsilon^2).
$$

The bracket is $[X,Y]=XY-YX$. To see that $\Lie(G)$ is closed under the
bracket, note that over $L[\epsilon,\eta]/(\epsilon^2,\eta^2)$ the
commutator of $1+\epsilon X$ and $1+\eta Y$ is $1+\epsilon\eta[X,Y]$. The
differential of a representation $r\colon G\to\GL(M)$ is characterized by

$$
r(1+\epsilon X)=1+\epsilon\,dr(X).
$$

These formulas show that $dr$ is a Lie algebra homomorphism.

Let $G$ be a connected algebraic group and $r\colon G\to\GL(M)$ an
algebraic representation. A subspace of $M$ is $G$-stable if and only if
it is $\Lie(G)$-stable. Moreover, if $G$ is a closed subgroup of
$\GL(V)$, then

$$
\Lie\bigl(Z(G)^\circ\bigr)=Z\bigl(\Lie(G)\bigr),
$$

with the Lie algebras computed by dual numbers as above and
$\Lie(Z(G)^\circ)$ regarded as a subspace of $\Lie(G)$ via the
differential of the inclusion $Z(G)^\circ\subseteq G$.

proof.text:
Let $U\subseteq M$ be a subspace. In a basis of $M$ extending a basis of
$U$, the scheme-theoretic stabilizer $S\subseteq G$ of $U$ is the closed
subgroup defined by the vanishing of the lower-left block of $r(g)$.
Differentiating these equations, we find

$$
\Lie(S)=\{X\in\Lie(G):dr(X)U\subseteq U\}.
$$

If $U$ is $\Lie(G)$-stable, then $\Lie(S)=\Lie(G)$, so Cartier's theorem
[sk-i-cartier] gives $\dim S=\dim\Lie(S)=\dim\Lie(G)=\dim G$, and the
dimension criterion of [sk-p-geometry] shows that $S=G$. Conversely, if
$U$ is $G$-stable, then $S=G$, and the displayed formula shows that $U$
is $\Lie(G)$-stable.

Now let $G\subseteq\GL(V)$ be a closed subgroup and put
$\mathfrak g=\Lie(G)$. We claim that the kernel of the adjoint
representation $G\to\GL(\mathfrak g)$ is the center. Indeed, if $g$ acts
trivially on $\mathfrak g$, then the centralizer $C_G(g)$ is a closed
subgroup of $G$ with Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, so it equals $G$ by the
Lie criterion of [sk-p-geometry]. Conversely, a central element acts trivially. Since the
kernel and the center are reduced by Cartier's theorem [sk-i-cartier],
their equality on $L$-points is an equality of schemes. Finally, the
formula

$$
\operatorname{Ad}(1+\epsilon X)(Y)=Y+\epsilon[X,Y]
$$

shows that $\Lie(Z(G))=\ker(\operatorname{ad})=Z(\mathfrak g)$, and
$Z(G)^\circ$ has the same Lie algebra as $Z(G)$ by [sk-i-cartier].
